prompt: Evaluate the relative importance of the causes of European maritime exploration in the period c. 1450–1750.

groups.label: Profit: gold, spices and new trade routes
Religion: spreading Christianity and fighting Muslim powers
Royal sponsorship, rivalry and navigation technology

pool.sourcing: Zurara was Portugal's royal chronicler and an admirer of Prince Henry, so he puts God's service first among Henry's reasons. Even so he admits that sailors went only where profit was certain and lists new markets as a reason, which makes the passage strong evidence that trade mattered even to the prince's own supporters.

Soncino was the Duke of Milan's envoy reporting what he heard at the English court, so this is secondhand news of Cabot's plans. It shows the hope of making London a greater spice market than Alexandria, which is good evidence of what backers wanted and weaker evidence of what the voyage achieved.

The letter was written down for the Zamorin by the Portuguese Diogo Dias, and it survives only as its general sense reported in the journal of da Gama's voyage, so the wording passed through Portuguese hands. It still shows an Indian ruler treating the Portuguese as ordinary traders who must pay in gold, silver, coral and cloth, which supports an economic reading of what drew them to India.

Zainuddin was a Muslim scholar of Malabar writing about eighty-five years after da Gama's arrival, in a history that urged Muslims to fight the Portuguese. He did not witness 1498 and repeats what the Portuguese said 'according to their own accounts'. Still, his view from India that they came to buy pepper at its source is a useful check on European claims of religious purpose.

A papal bull is a legal grant, and this one gave Portugal rights in Africa, so the pope had reason to describe the voyages as a holy effort to reach Christians in the Indies and fight the 'Saracens'. It is strong evidence of how the Church justified exploration and weaker evidence of what sailors and merchants wanted.

Columbus addressed this prologue to Ferdinand and Isabella, who sponsored the voyage, in 1492, the year they completed the conquest of Granada, so he describes the mission in the crusading terms they would welcome. It shows the religious language of royal sponsorship, though Columbus's other writings for the same rulers stress gold.

The speech is known from the Commentaries that Albuquerque's son compiled from his papers and published in 1557 to honour him, so the wording may be polished. Albuquerque gives driving out the Moors as his first reason and seizing the spice trade as his second, which makes the speech good evidence that religious and economic aims were joined and weak evidence that either one came first.

The Christian emperor of Ethiopia wrote to King Manuel around 1522 as one Christian ruler to another, proposing that they assist one another in lands he describes as full of Moors and pagans. It shows from the African side that the Christian ruler Portugal had long hoped to find was real, though he may have had his own reasons for welcoming Portuguese settlers on his coast, which the letter does not spell out.

This is a royal grant written before the voyage, a legal promise of titles and power to Columbus if he discovered and conquered lands. It is strong evidence that the crown sponsored the voyage and expected to rule new lands, and it says little about trade or conversion.

The daily entries survive only in Bartolomé de las Casas's abstract of the journal, much of it his own paraphrase, so the words are not exactly Columbus's. The passage is still useful evidence that charts, latitudes, compass readings and careful records made the crossing possible, and it shows how frightening the open ocean was to the crew.

A member of da Gama's crew reports what da Gama told the Zamorin, a ruler he needed to impress, so the claim that Portugal sought Christian kings and had no need of gold or silver was diplomacy. Its stronger evidence is the sixty years of royal voyages and King Manuel's orders, which show steady sponsorship by the Portuguese crown.

Hakluyt wrote this at Walter Raleigh's request to persuade Queen Elizabeth I to back English colonies, so he gathers every argument that might win her support. His stress on weakening King Philip of Spain and strengthening the navy shows rivalry between states driving English expansion by the 1580s, next to Protestant and trade arguments.

thesis: Economic motives were the most important cause, because the search for spices, gold and new trade routes explains why voyages continued for three centuries and drew in merchants and later trading companies: Zurara admits that sailors went only where profit was certain, Cabot hoped to make London a spice market, and Indian observers such as the Zamorin and Zainuddin saw the Portuguese as traders who had come for pepper and spices.

Religious motives were the most important cause of the first voyages of the 1400s, because Portugal and Spain came out of centuries of war against Muslim states: the pope, Prince Henry's chronicler and Columbus all present exploration as a way to find Christian allies and convert new peoples, and the Ethiopian emperor's letter shows such allies existed. Economic aims grew in weight once the sea route to Asia was open.

State sponsorship and rivalry were the decisive cause, because the wish for spices and converts was old and became voyages only when monarchs paid for ships and new navigation methods made long ocean crossings possible: Ferdinand and Isabella's grant to Columbus, sixty years of Portuguese royal voyages and Hakluyt's case against Spain show crowns driving exploration to gain land and power.

contextualization.text: Before 1500, Asian spices reached Europe through Arab merchants and then Venice, which dominated the Mediterranean end of the trade and made very large profits. No European ruler had broken that hold, so states facing the Atlantic began looking for a sea route to the spice lands.

The Reconquista, the long war of Christian kingdoms against Muslim rulers in Iberia, ended in 1492 when Ferdinand and Isabella conquered Granada. Popes had backed some of these campaigns, which helps explain why Spanish and Portuguese sources describe voyages as a fight against 'Moors' and 'Saracens'.

Portugal began its overseas expansion by capturing the Moroccan port of Ceuta in 1415. Prince Henry, who fought there, later used the funds of the Order of Christ to pay for voyages down the West African coast that sought gold, enslaved people and new colonies such as Madeira.

outsideEvidence.text: Lateen sail: this triangular sail, spread through the Mediterranean by Arab sailors, let ships tack into the wind, and combined with square sails it produced ocean-going ships, which supports the argument that borrowed technology made the voyages possible.

Mariner's astrolabe: Portuguese navigators perfected this instrument for finding a ship's latitude from the height of the sun or a star, which helped captains know their position on long voyages far from the coast.

Bartolomeu Dias, 1488: sent by King John II, Dias led the first European expedition around the Cape of Good Hope and opened a sea route to Asia, which shows decades of royal sponsorship paying off before da Gama reached India.

Treaty of Tordesillas, 1494: Spain and Portugal moved the pope's dividing line to 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, which shows rivalry between states shaping exploration; the new line later let Portugal claim Brazil.

Prester John: Europeans told stories of a Christian king living among pagans and Muslims, and in 1487 Portugal sent the envoys Pêro da Covilhã and Afonso de Paiva overland both to learn about a sea route to India and to ask about him, which shows religious and commercial goals pursued together.

Dutch East India Company, 1602: the Dutch state gave this company a trade monopoly from the Cape of Good Hope to the Strait of Magellan and the right to make treaties, build forts and keep armed forces, which shows profit and state power driving voyages in the 1600s.

complexity: Show that the motives were tied together: Albuquerque gives a religious and a commercial reason in the same speech, and Zurara lists both profit and the faith among Henry's reasons, so a strong essay can argue that religion often justified voyages that profit kept going.

Explain change over time: crusading language fills the Portuguese and Spanish sources of the 1400s, while in 1584 Hakluyt gives trade, the navy and weakening Spain as much weight as religion, and the Dutch and English companies of the 1600s were founded for trade, so the relative importance of the causes shifted across the period.

Use point of view across groups: European sources written for kings and popes stress God's service, while the Zamorin treats the Portuguese as merchants and Zainuddin says they came for pepper, so sources from Asia qualify the religious explanation.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which European states relied on violence rather than negotiation and alliance to build maritime empires in the period c. 1450–1750.

groups.label: Force: conquest, forts, bombardment and massacre
Negotiation: alliances, treaties and local rulers setting terms

pool.sourcing: The Requerimiento was a legal text drafted for the Spanish crown to be read before conquest, and it ends by blaming the victims for any deaths, so its offer of peace was a legal formality. It is strong evidence that the crown planned for war and enslavement and weak evidence of how Indigenous peoples responded.

Díaz was a soldier in Cortés's army writing about fifty years later, partly to defend the record of the ordinary conquerors, so he justifies the massacre as a needed 'example'. The passage is still useful because it shows Spanish violence carried out together with Tlaxcalan allies, who joined the fighting and plunder.

Mayr was a German clerk with Almeida's fleet who saw these events, and he reports the seizure of envoys, the plunder and the new fort without apology. That makes his account strong evidence that the Portuguese used force to build forts on the East African coast, even after the sheikh offered to pay tribute.

The Malay Annals is the court chronicle of the Malacca sultans, compiled about a century after the Portuguese attacks, so it remembers them through the defeated court's eyes and runs separate attacks together. Its picture of terror at cannon fire shows how the court remembered Portuguese ship artillery, but Malacca had guns of its own, so it is weaker evidence of what decided the battle.

Zainuddin, a Muslim scholar of Malabar, wrote to rouse Muslims against the Portuguese and explains their arrival as God's punishment, so he stresses cruelty and forced conversion. His account is valuable as the victims' view of seized ships and profaned mosques, and it is better evidence of what Muslim merchants suffered than of Portuguese policy as a whole.

This anonymous account describes wrongs done by the Dutch to English traders, and its authors' purpose and sympathies are not known, so it gives no Dutch side. It shows Europeans using force against each other to control the spice trade, and it also shows the governor of Bantam forbidding fighting in his harbour, a limit set by a local ruler.

Díaz reconstructs the Tlaxcalan general's speech from memory decades later, so the words are his version. It shows the Tlaxcalans choosing alliance to escape Mexica raids, which supports the importance of local partners, while Cortés's threat to destroy their town shows the alliance also rested on force.

A member of da Gama's crew records that Calicut's officials laughed at the Portuguese gifts and made them follow local custom. Because a Portuguese writer admits this embarrassment, the passage is strong evidence that Indian rulers and merchants set the terms of the first contact.

Sidi Ali Reis was an Ottoman admiral stranded in Gujarat after a sea battle with the Portuguese, so he is hostile to them and keen to show Gujarat's loyalty to the Ottoman sultan. He still shows a rebel noble offering the Portuguese harbours in return for their aid and Gujarat's ministers refusing a Portuguese demand, which supports the role of alliance and local politics.

Jahangir writes as a far greater ruler granting favours to a distant king, and the surviving English version is a copy in Roe's hand, so the friendly tone is diplomatic. It is strong evidence that the English gained trading rights in India by royal permission and gifts.

Roe was writing advice to the East India Company, whose trade he was sent to secure, so he argues for what would serve the Company's profits. His claim that forts and land wars ruined the Portuguese and Dutch is an opinion, but it shows an English official choosing trade over force in Mughal India.

Powhatan's words come through John Smith's Generall Historie of 1624, written fifteen years later in a book that promoted both the colony and Smith's own role, so the speech may be shaped by Smith. It still records a Native ruler setting the terms of trade and warning that force would leave the English hungry.

thesis: Europeans relied mainly on violence where they held a military edge, at sea and on lightly defended coasts and islands: Portuguese cannon terrified Malacca, Almeida's fleet plundered Kilwa and built a fort, and the Requerimiento set out a legal formula for war and enslavement in the Americas.

Europeans relied on negotiation and alliance more than on violence, because powerful local rulers controlled access to trade and land: Calicut's officials set the terms of da Gama's visit, Jahangir granted the English trade on his own terms, and in Mexico the Tlaxcalan alliance was essential to the conquest.

The balance between force and negotiation depended on local power and changed over time: Iberian conquerors of the 1500s used force widely, but by the 1600s English agents such as Roe judged forts and land wars too costly against strong Asian states, while violence continued where Europeans faced weaker states or one another, as the Dutch attacks on English ships show.

contextualization.text: Before the Portuguese arrived in 1498, Muslim merchants dominated trade across the Indian Ocean: Gujaratis carried spices from the Moluccas and silk from China, and Calicut was the centre of pepper exports to the Red Sea. Europeans entered a rich trading system that already had its own rulers and customs.

The Reconquista, in which Christian kingdoms took Iberia from Muslim rulers, ended at Granada in 1492. It gave Spain and Portugal a long tradition of war for land and faith, and popes had backed some of its campaigns.

In India, Europeans met the Mughal dynasty, which ruled most of northern India from the early 1500s to the mid-1700s. European trading companies were far too weak to conquer such a land empire before the mid-1700s.

outsideEvidence.text: Cartaz system: from 1502 the Portuguese required merchant ships in the Indian Ocean to carry their pass and pay duties at posts such as Goa, Malacca and Hormuz, and ships without one risked seizure or sinking, which shows naval force used to tax a trade run mostly by Asian merchants.
Battle of Diu, 1509: Francisco de Almeida burned and pillaged ports and defeated the combined Arab and Egyptian fleet off Diu, which shows naval force at the centre of Portuguese expansion.

Portuguese conquest of Goa, 1510: Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa from the Adil Shahi sultanate on the advice of Timoja, said to be an admiral of the Vijayanagar fleet, and with help from Goa's Hindu population, which shows conquest itself depending on local allies.

Cajamarca, 1532: Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than 200 men, ambushed and captured the Inca ruler Atahuallpa, took a ransom of gold and silver and executed him in 1533, which shows violence toppling an empire already weakened by civil war.

Malinche (Doña Marina): one of a group of enslaved women given to the Spaniards by the Tabascans in 1519, she became Cortés's interpreter in Maya and Nahuatl, and his success often depended directly on her, which shows conquest relying on Indigenous go-betweens.

The Dutch at Dejima: after the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637–38 the Tokugawa shogunate expelled the Portuguese in 1639 and in 1641 confined the Dutch to Dejima, a fenced island in Nagasaki harbour guarded at night, which shows Europeans keeping their trade only by accepting an Asian state's terms.

complexity: Corroborate across groups: force and alliance often worked together, since the Cholula massacre was carried out with Tlaxcalan allies and a rebel noble in Gujarat offered the Portuguese his harbours in return for their help, so several documents support both lines of argument.

Compare regions: in the Americas small Spanish forces with Indigenous allies overthrew large empires, while in Asia Europeans used force mainly at sea and had to bargain with land empires such as the Mughals or accept limits such as Dejima.

Weigh point of view: European writers such as Díaz and Mayr present violence as normal or necessary, while the Malay Annals and Zainuddin describe it from the victims' side, so an essay that sources both qualifies any single answer about how much Europeans relied on force.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Columbian Exchange changed societies in the Americas, Africa and Europe in the period 1492–1750.

pool.sourcing: This part of the Kaqchikel annals was written by a family member who lived through the epidemic and addresses later generations as 'my children', so it records the loss as family and community memory. It is strong evidence that disease killed rulers and elders and left the kingdom poor, though it does not name the disease or say where it came from.

This Maya community record lists events by katun in a few words, so it gives order and dates more than explanation. By setting 'the general death' and smallpox beside the arrival of foreigners, baptism and Spanish officials, it shows Maya scribes remembering disease as part of the whole change brought by colonial rule.

Díaz, a soldier with Cortés, traces the epidemic to an African servant of Narváez and blames Indigenous remedies, which turns attention away from the Spaniards. His account still shows smallpox killing many lords and letting Cortés choose their successors, evidence that disease changed political power in Mexico.

Winthrop kept this journal as governor of a Puritan colony that looked for God's hand in events, so he takes care to note Native people praising 'the Englishmen's God'. His record of Native leaders and nearly whole villages dying and of trade stopping is strong evidence that disease changed Native societies in New England.

Garcilaso, son of a conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, wrote in Spain decades later from memories of his childhood in Cuzco. His account of crowds of Indians amazed by plough oxen and of cattle prices collapsing is vivid evidence of change in the Andes, though it reflects what one boy saw in one city.

Acosta was a Jesuit who lived in Peru and Mexico and wrote a natural history for European readers, so he sorts and counts animals with a scholar's eye. His figures for hides unloaded at Seville from the 1587 fleet show European animals changing American land and sending wealth back to Europe.

Pigafetta, an Italian writer, set down what the Portuguese merchant Duarte Lopes told him about Kongo, so the report is secondhand and comes from a European trader. Its note that people in Kongo called maize 'Portugal grain' and fed it to pigs shows an American crop had reached Africa by the 1580s but was not yet valued there.

King James wrote this attack to turn his subjects against tobacco, so he exaggerates its harm and insults Native Americans. His complaint that gentlemen spent hundreds of pounds a year on it is strong evidence that an American plant had already changed English habits by 1604.

Ligon helped manage a Barbados sugar plantation and wrote for English readers interested in the island, so he describes enslaved people as property to be looked after. His list of enslaved Africans, European cattle and horses, and American crops such as cassava on one estate shows how the exchange built a new plantation economy.

Gândavo wrote his history of Brazil to encourage Portuguese people to settle there, so he makes colonial life sound easy. That purpose makes him reliable on what settlers wanted, enslaved Indigenous workers for sugar mills and farms, and unreliable on how hard the work was.

Philips was a sailor on Hawkins's slaving voyage who wrote his account after returning to England in 1582, and he presents the raid as ordinary business. His account shows an African king's war supplying captives for sale in the Spanish Caribbean, linking African warfare to labour demand in the Americas.

Hawks was an English merchant writing at the request of the English lawyer Richard Hakluyt the elder, so he describes a rival empire for English readers. His report that mines declined once Indigenous slaves were freed and few Indians were left shows population loss and royal law reshaping the labour system.

thesis: Disease changed societies in the Americas more than any other part of the exchange, because epidemics killed rulers and most of the population and opened the way to conquest: the Kaqchikel annals, Díaz and Winthrop all describe leaders and whole villages dying, from Guatemala to New England.

Before 1750 the exchange changed the Americas far more than Africa or Europe: European livestock and crops remade American land and work, while in Kongo maize was still fed to pigs in the 1580s, and in Europe new habits such as tobacco spread quickly but staple crops such as the potato took hold in most of Europe only in the 1700s.

The most far-reaching change was a new Atlantic labour system linking all three continents: population collapse and new cash crops pushed colonists to enslave Indigenous people and then Africans, as Hawks, Gândavo, Philips and Ligon show, so African wars and European markets were tied to American plantations.

contextualization.text: Before 1492, Native Americans had never been exposed to the infectious diseases long common in Eurasia and Africa, such as smallpox, measles and influenza, because the two hemispheres had been separated for thousands of years. When Columbus's voyages reconnected them, these diseases spread as epidemics among Native American populations.

By the late 1400s Portuguese ships were carrying enslaved Africans to sugar plantations on Atlantic islands such as Madeira, and Spanish conquerors took enslaved Africans to the Caribbean after 1502. In the 1600s demand rose sharply with the growth of sugar plantations in the Caribbean and tobacco in the Chesapeake.

outsideEvidence.text: Potato in Europe: brought from the Andes by the Spanish in the late 1500s, it became a major crop in Ireland by the end of the 1600s and in continental Europe by the end of the 1700s, which shows Europe changed too, but mostly late in the period.

Cassava in Africa: this root crop from Brazil reached Africa in the 1500s, became a staple food in Angola and Kongo, and could be left in the ground so that farmers could flee slave raiders, which shows American crops changing African societies.

Horses on the Great Plains: the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 put thousands of Spanish horses in Native hands, many were traded north, and by the 1730s the Comanche were fully mounted, which shows Old World animals transforming Native societies beyond Spanish control.
Malaria and yellow fever: these diseases crossed the Atlantic from Africa to the Americas, which shows the disease side of the exchange tied Africa to the Americas as well as Europe.

Encomienda: Spanish grants of the tribute and labour of Indigenous people, defined in law in 1503, lost their value as the Indigenous population collapsed and were gradually replaced by large landed estates (haciendas), which links disease directly to changes in labour.

complexity: Compare the three regions: the Americas lost most of their people and gained new animals, Africa lost people to the slave trade but gained crops such as maize and cassava, and Europe gained new goods such as hides and tobacco, so the exchange changed all three in very different ways.

Show change over time: early sources show slow acceptance, with maize fed to pigs in Kongo in the 1580s and the potato a major crop in continental Europe only by the end of the 1700s, so a claim about the extent of change should separate the 1500s from the 1700s.

Qualify with point of view: Puritan governors read epidemics as God's favour and Díaz blames Indigenous remedies, while Bartolomé de las Casas blamed Spanish violence and forced labour for the collapse, so a careful essay weighs disease against conquest.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which social hierarchies in the Spanish and Portuguese Americas changed in the period 1500–1750.

groups.label: Moving up or down the hierarchy

pool.sourcing: Garcilaso was himself a mestizo, son of a conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, writing in Spain, and he defends the word 'mestizo' with pride. That makes him strong evidence that new mixed categories were invented after the conquest and that each group gave them different meanings.

Gage, an English former friar who turned Protestant, wrote for English readers hostile to Spain, so he plays up quarrels inside Spanish society. His account of creoles kept from high office and insulted as 'half Indians' describes a real divide between American-born and Spanish-born Spaniards, though he may exaggerate its bitterness.

Juan and Ulloa were Spanish naval officers sent by the king, so they describe colonial society as visitors from Spain. Their remark that light-skinned mestizos were counted as Spaniards within two or three generations is strong evidence that by 1748 racial categories could shift with appearance.

Vázquez de Espinosa, a Spanish friar who travelled through Spanish America, lists Cuzco's people in order from knights and encomenderos down to enslaved Africans, so he shows the hierarchy as a Spaniard saw it. His praise of mestizo soldiers in the king's service hints that mixed-race men could win some standing.

Nakuk Pech was a Maya chief writing the history of his own town, and he stresses his loyalty, his baptism and the titles his family received. That emphasis makes the account strong evidence that some Indigenous nobles kept their rank under Spanish rule by cooperating as tribute collectors and hidalgos.

This royal decree answers a petition from the poor son of a conquistador, so it shows what the crown chose to reward: service in the conquest. It is good evidence that conquerors' families could fall into poverty and that their status depended on royal favour, though it describes a single case.

Vázquez de Espinosa describes the defences of Cartagena and Lima and praises the free colored companies as 'as good as Spaniards'. It shows free men of African descent gaining a recognised place in royal service, though their separate companies kept them marked as a distinct group.

Gândavo wrote to persuade Portuguese people to settle in Brazil, so he makes it sound easy for a poor man to rise. His claim that owning a few slaves let a settler live 'in a respectable way' shows that in Portuguese Brazil a European's standing rose through owning enslaved people.

Las Casas, a Dominican friar and former encomienda holder, wrote to persuade the crown to stop Spanish abuses, so he describes the system at its worst. His account is strong evidence of how the first encomiendas worked on Hispaniola and less reliable for numbers.

The New Laws are royal legislation, so they show what the crown wanted: an end to Indian slavery and to encomiendas passing to heirs. Settlers' opposition weakened them, which makes the law strong evidence of attempted change from the top and weak evidence of what happened in practice.

A Kaqchikel noble who lived through these years writes for his descendants about Alvarado's demands for gold-washing labour and his naming of rulers at will, then praises President Cerrato for freeing slaves and ending forced labour. The account shows both the coerced labour imposed on Maya people and the real change a royal official could bring.

Gândavo writes as a promoter of Brazil and credits the Jesuits with ending 'disorder' in the slave trade, so he may overstate the reform. His account shows both continuity, since captives taken in a 'just war' stayed slaves, and change, since inspections freed people enslaved illegally.

thesis: Social hierarchies changed in form more than in their basic order: new categories such as creole, mestizo and mulatto appeared, yet people of Spanish descent stayed at the top while Indigenous and African people did the coerced labour, as Garcilaso, Vázquez de Espinosa and Gage show.

Hierarchies changed significantly, because mixing and royal service opened new routes to status: Maya nobles became hidalgos, free men of African descent served in royal militia companies, and by 1748 light-skinned mestizos in Quito were counted as Spaniards.

Coerced labour shows only limited change: the New Laws and officials such as Cerrato ended some Indigenous slavery and encomienda abuses, but new labour drafts and the growing enslavement of Africans kept the people at the bottom working for others throughout the period.

contextualization.text: In Castile and Portugal, 'purity of blood' statutes from 1449 onward kept people of Jewish or Muslim descent out of many institutions. In Spain's American colonies the idea came to mean racial purity, and proofs of it were required in many cases, including for office.

Spain ruled its American lands through viceroyalties. The Viceroyalty of Peru, created in 1543, was long its most valuable possession because of the silver of Potosí, and mine operators and merchants lived richly in Lima on the forced labour of Indians.

Epidemics cut Native American populations by very large shares by 1650 (estimates range from about 50 to 95 percent, depending on the region) and almost wiped out the Indigenous peoples of most Caribbean islands by 1600, so colonists in the Caribbean and Brazil in particular turned increasingly to enslaved Africans.

outsideEvidence.text: Mita: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo expanded the old Inca labour draft to supply the Potosí silver mines, with the first draftees arriving in 1573, which shows an Andean institution kept but turned to Spanish purposes.

Repartimiento: under this crown-licensed system colonists drafted a share of a district's Indigenous people for periods of forced labour; the crown reformed it in 1601 and 1609, but forced drafts went on, which shows law changing faster than practice.

Hacienda: as the Indigenous population fell and farming replaced mining, the encomienda was gradually replaced by the hacienda system of large landed estates, so elite power came to rest on owning land.

African slavery in Brazil: Brazil imported more enslaved Africans than any other country, beginning in the mid-1500s, while the enslavement of Indigenous people continued into the 1600s and 1700s, which shows the Portuguese hierarchy resting on both.

Valladolid debate, 1550–51: the Spanish king halted further conquest while scholars debated whether the conquest and the treatment of Indigenous people were just, which shows the crown questioning the place of Indigenous people in colonial society.

complexity: Compare Spanish and Portuguese America: in Brazil owning slaves made a settler respectable and Jesuit inspections only partly limited Indigenous slavery, while Spanish America developed detailed mixed-race categories and royal offices, so both kept Europeans on top in different ways.

Show change over time: sources from the 1500s describe conquerors dividing Indigenous people among themselves as labourers, while the 1748 account of Quito shows categories that could shift with skin colour, so the hierarchy grew more complex and somewhat more fluid by the end of the period.

Weigh law against practice: royal decrees such as the New Laws and Philip II's cédula show what the crown intended, while observers such as Gage and Las Casas show abuses continuing, so an essay can qualify claims of change by asking whose view each source gives.

prompt: Evaluate the effects of the Atlantic slave trade on African states and societies in the period c. 1450–1750.

groups.label: Harm: violence, depopulation and broken states
Power: African rulers and elites who controlled the trade
Change: guns, law and social structure

pool.sourcing: Pigafetta set down the account of Duarte Lopes, a Portuguese merchant who lived in Kongo, so the report gives a trader's view of the Jaga invasion and the famine that followed. It shows starving people selling their own relatives to Portuguese merchants from São Tomé, evidence that war and the trade together harmed Kongo.

Battell was an English sailor held by the Portuguese who lived among the Imbangala, and his account was printed by Samuel Purchas years later. He took part in loading slaves himself and reports the cheap captives and the defeat of the Benguelas and the death of their ruler plainly, which makes it strong evidence of harm to African states.

Barbot was an agent of the French Royal African Company writing for European readers, and his remark 'so inhuman are the Blacks to one another' shifts blame onto Africans. Even so, his description of children kidnapped from fields, famine victims selling themselves and captives starved on the march is evidence of the trade's harm to ordinary people.

Bluett, an English lawyer, wrote down Ayuba's story for English readers, so the words pass through him, but the events come from an African who was enslaved. Ayuba had just sold two slaves of his own when raiders seized him, which shows raiding endangering even traders and elites.

Cadamosto was a Venetian merchant sailing for Prince Henry who wanted to sell horses, so he judges Budomel as a business partner. His account shows a Wolof ruler buying on credit and setting where payment in slaves would be made, evidence that African rulers controlled the terms from the start.

Leo Africanus, a Muslim scholar and diplomat from Fez, describes Bornu's trade of horses for slaves with merchants from across the Sahara. It shows that slave raiding already made some African kings rich before the Atlantic trade grew, so it is evidence of continuity and cannot by itself show an Atlantic effect.

Phillips was an English slave-ship captain who complains that he had to pay more for the king's poorer slaves, and a captain had no reason to invent being pushed around by an African king. His journal is strong evidence that Whydah's king taxed European ships, set terms and profited.

Barbot made slaving voyages for a French company in 1678–82, and his account was printed in English in 1732, about fifty years later; he describes Africans as the sellers and says little about European pressure. His report that kings, rich men and leading merchants ran the trade and carried European goods far inland on credit is useful evidence of elite control, read with his point of view in mind.

Bosman was the Dutch West India Company's chief merchant at Elmina, and he admits selling guns that could be turned on the Dutch because rival Europeans would sell them anyway. Because he admits a trade he thought dangerous to the Dutch, the passage is strong evidence that firearms became a chief import of the Gold Coast.

Snelgrave was a slave-ship captain who wrote to defend the trade, so his claim that Africans once killed surplus captives and now sold them is self-serving. The passage is best used as evidence of how slavers justified the trade, and only as weak evidence of how warfare changed.

Moore worked on the Gambia for the Royal African Company, which bought slaves there, so he had no reason to make the trade look worse than it was. His report that even trifling crimes came to be punished by sale into slavery is strong evidence that the trade changed African law.

Battell writes about his own life among the Imbangala, where his musket made him valuable to their war leader. It shows firearms changing warfare and African merchants coming to war camps to buy captives, though it is one man's experience around 1600.

thesis: The Atlantic slave trade mainly harmed African states and societies, because raids, wars and famine sales destroyed communities and states: people in Kongo sold relatives during famine, Imbangala war bands defeated the Benguelas and killed their ruler, and even a trader like Ayuba could be seized.

The trade's effects depended on a society's position in it: coastal and military states such as Whydah and Dahomey grew rich by controlling supply and taxing Europeans, while their neighbours and ordinary people were raided, so the trade strengthened some states as it weakened others.

The trade changed African institutions as well as population: guns became a chief import on the Gold Coast, law along the Gambia turned crimes into reasons for sale, and wars were increasingly fought to take captives.

contextualization.text: Long before 1450, enslaved Africans were carried across the Sahara to North Africa, and Berber traders exchanged horses from Morocco for slaves from the Jolof kingdom. The Atlantic trade added new buyers to an older system.

The Portuguese built Elmina, the first European stone fort on the Gold Coast, in 1482 on a site leased from local states. In the 1600s Dutch, English and other traders turned these coastal ties toward exporting slaves, and by the mid-1700s about 40 European forts stood on the coast.

An estimated 10 to 12 million enslaved Africans were shipped across the Atlantic from the 1500s to the 1800s. Probably no more than a few hundred thousand were taken before 1600; demand rose sharply with Caribbean sugar in the 1600s, and roughly half of the trade took place in the 1700s.

outsideEvidence.text: Afonso I of Kongo: in 1526 he wrote to the king of Portugal protesting that traders, helped by some Kongo nobles, were kidnapping free people, even sons of nobles and members of his own family, which shows the trade weakening royal authority.

Dahomey: King Agaja, eager to buy European arms, conquered Allada in 1724 and Whydah in 1727, and the kingdom was organised for war to take captives, who were sold for weapons or set to work on royal plantations, which shows the trade building a powerful state. (Snelgrave's source line names Agaja only as the king he visited, so only the conquests and the war-making state count as outside evidence.)

Asante: from the early 1700s the Asante supplied enslaved people to British and Dutch traders and received firearms, which they used to expand their territory, an example of the exchange of slaves for guns strengthening a state.

Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba: after Portuguese wars that burned villages and seized captives in Ndongo, she allied with Imbangala forces and later the Dutch, conquered Matamba in 1631–35 and fought the Portuguese until a peace treaty in 1656, which shows African rulers resisting and adapting.

Cassava: this American crop reached Africa in the 1500s and could be left in the ground for months, so farmers targeted by raiders could flee and return, and it became a staple food in Angola and Kongo.
Loss of young adults: many captives were young men and women of childbearing age, while the old and dependent were left behind, which weakened families and local economies.

complexity: Show continuity with older trade: Cadamosto and Leo Africanus show rulers exchanging slaves for horses with traders from across the Sahara, so the Atlantic trade grew out of existing systems even as it greatly increased their scale.

Corroborate across groups: the rulers who gained most, such as Dahomey's kings, did so by making war on their neighbours, and Whydah itself was conquered by Dahomey in 1727, so harm and power were two sides of the same process.

Source the European writers: slavers such as Snelgrave and Barbot had reasons to blame Africans or defend the trade, while Ayuba's account comes from a victim through an English recorder, so weighing point of view shows why historians still debate how far Europeans and Africans each drove the trade.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the global silver trade transformed economies in the period 1550–1750.

groups.label: Mining and forced labour in the Americas
Silver flowing to China through Manila
Prices, royal finance and bullion debates in Europe

pool.sourcing: Cieza was a Spanish soldier and chronicler who saw Potosí in 1549, in its first boom, when mine owners paid Indigenous workers in silver and Andean wind furnaces smelted the ore. That timing makes the passage good evidence of how fast silver drew people to Potosí, but it cannot show the forced labour draft and mercury refining that came later.

Acosta, a Spanish Jesuit who lived in Peru and visited Potosí, writes for European readers and counts the king's profit from mercury with approval, mentioning the danger to workers only at the end. That makes the passage strong evidence that amalgamation after 1571 made poor ore worth mining and enriched the crown, and weaker evidence of what it cost the workers.

Garcilaso, the son of a conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, wrote in Spain to honour Inca rule, so his picture of kings who banned mercury to protect their people is hard to check. Even so, his point that Andeans had no word for mercury until the Spanish found it is useful evidence that Spanish silver production broke sharply with Andean practice.

Vázquez de Espinosa was a Carmelite friar who travelled through Peru in the 1610s, and his sympathy for 'the poor Indians' leads him to stress abuses. His precise figures for the 13,300 men drafted each year make the passage strong evidence of the scale of the mita and the damage it did to Andean villages and their chiefs.

Chanchian, a Ming envoy, writes to calm the Spanish governor and says himself that the rumour of a gold and silver mountain is a lie. The letter is weak evidence about Luzon's riches but good evidence that the Ming court wanted silver enough to send officials after a rumour; it reaches us through a Dominican friar's Spanish version.

A Ming official writes to the Spanish governor after the 1603 massacre of Chinese in Manila, and he wants justice, payment and the return of survivors, so he stresses how much Chinese traders had built the colony. That purpose makes the letter strong evidence that the Chinese saw Manila's wealth as resting on their trade, though it comes to us through a Spanish translation made at the time.

Morga was a senior judge and lieutenant-governor in Manila, so he knew the trade closely but judged it as a Spanish official worried about the crown and the colony. His complaint that silver passed to 'infidels' and never returned shows Spanish fears, and his remark that Chinese merchants would take only silver is strong evidence of Chinese demand.

Grau represented Manila at the Spanish court, and in this passage he sets out the Seville merchants' case against the Manila trade, so these are the arguments of Manila's rivals. Read that way, it shows that Spanish merchants believed American silver ended up in China and that cheap Chinese silks hurt Spanish sales in America.

This royal decree speaks for the Spanish crown, which wanted American silver to reach Spain and its treasury, so it presents the Manila trade as a loss. Its admission that viceroys and governors let shipments exceed the limits is strong evidence that the crown could not control where its silver went.

Mun was a director of the East India Company, which shipped silver to Asia, so he had a stake in arguing that exporting money made England richer. His summary of the opposite view, held by the public and written into Spanish law, is good evidence of how highly most Europeans prized bullion.

North was a London merchant who had traded in the Ottoman Empire, and he writes to argue against laws that restrict trade. His claim that silver arriving from Spain is a commodity like any other shows that some Europeans were rejecting bullionism by 1691, though it is one merchant's argument.

Montesquieu wrote in 1748 as a French philosopher looking back over two centuries, and his aim was to show that gold and silver only represent wealth. His distance makes him a poor witness to events but strong evidence of how European thinkers judged American silver's effect on prices and on Spain.

thesis: The silver trade transformed economies to a great extent because it linked three regions: forced labour and mercury refining built a mining economy at Potosí, Chinese demand pulled the silver across the Pacific through Manila, and in Europe it raised prices and fed royal spending, so each region came to depend on silver mined or spent somewhere else.

The transformation was deepest in the Andes and in China and weakest in Spain: the mita and mercury reorganized Indigenous labour and emptied villages, and Chinese merchants drew silver into China, while Spanish officials and later writers such as Montesquieu complained that the silver passed through Spain without making it rich.

The silver trade transformed economies only to a limited extent, because older systems decided where the silver went and how it was used: the Ming state's own tax reforms created the demand for silver, the Spanish crown spent it on wars and debts, and by the mid-1600s Potosí's output was falling.

contextualization.text: Silver was discovered at Potosí in the Andes in 1545, and within about three decades the town had well over 100,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in the Americas.

Ming China's single whip reform, extended across the empire in the 1580s, turned most land taxes, poll taxes and labour duties into one payment in silver, which raised China's imports of silver from Japan and Spanish America.

From 1565 Spanish galleons usually sailed once a year in each direction between Acapulco and Manila, carrying American silver to Asia and Asian goods back, because silver was worth much more in Asia than in the Americas.

outsideEvidence.text: Zacatecas silver mines in New Spain: from the mid-1500s they were among the largest sources of wealth in Spain's colonies, which shows that silver transformed northern Mexico as well as the Andes.
Iwami Ginzan silver mine in Japan: it peaked in the early 1600s, and Japanese silver was used in trade with China, Portugal and the Netherlands, which shows that China also drew silver from Japan.

Spanish dollar (piece of eight): this silver coin of the Spanish Empire, minted at places such as Mexico City, became the first widely used international currency, which shows how far American silver spread through world trade.
Philip II's loan defaults: despite American silver, the Spanish crown defaulted on its loans in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596, which supports the argument that silver did not secure Spain's finances.

Casa de Contratación: this royal trading house in Seville, founded in 1503, scheduled ships and routes, collected duties and kept royal revenues, which shows how the Spanish crown tried to channel American wealth into its treasury.

complexity: Corroborate across groups: Morga in Manila and Philip III in Spain both complain that silver went to 'infidel' lands, while the Ming official and Chanchian show the Chinese side of the same flow, so writers with very different aims agree on the direction of the trade.

Qualify with a counter-argument: Mun defended sending silver abroad, North treated silver as a commodity like any other, and Montesquieu argued that more silver only raised prices, so an essay can argue that silver changed prices and trade routes more than it created lasting wealth for Spain.

Connect to a later period: China's demand for silver lasted into the 1800s, and when British merchants began selling Indian opium in China to pay for tea, silver started to flow out of China, a dispute that helped cause the Opium War of 1839–42.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which mercantilism shaped how European states and joint-stock companies ran their empires in the period 1600–1750.

groups.label: State laws to keep trade and bullion at home

pool.sourcing: This royal decree speaks for the Spanish crown, which limited the Manila trade because silver was leaving for 'infidel kingdoms' and harming the treasury and Spain's own trade with the Indies. It shows Spain acting on mercantilist fears, and its admission that viceroys and governors let the limits be exceeded shows that the crown could not enforce its own rules.

As a law passed by Parliament, the Navigation Act states what the English state intended: goods from Asia, Africa and America were to arrive only in English ships with mostly English crews, a rule aimed at the Dutch carrying trade. It is strong evidence of policy, but a law cannot show how well it was obeyed.

Mun, a London merchant and East India Company director, wrote this as advice on how England could grow rich, and it was published after his death in 1664. It is strong evidence of the mercantilist rule that a kingdom must sell more abroad than it buys, though it describes an ideal and gives no real trade figures.

North was a merchant who had traded in the Ottoman Empire and later served as a Treasury commissioner, and he writes to argue that laws restricting trade do not make a nation rich. As a critic, he is evidence that mercantilist policy was being questioned in England by the 1690s, though his view was not yet the policy of any state.

The States General wrote this charter to grant the company its powers, so it shows the Dutch state's plan: a company that could make alliances, build forts and appoint governors in the state's name. It is strong evidence that companies acted as arms of the state, though a charter records intentions, so it cannot show what the company actually did.

Roe, the English ambassador at the Mughal court, writes privately to advise the East India Company against forts and land wars. His letter shows that some English agents thought profit came from 'quiet trade' at sea, and his criticism of Portuguese and Dutch garrisons shows that rivals chose force.

Jahangir writes as a great emperor granting favour to a distant king, letting English merchants trade freely in his ports and asking for rare goods for his palace. The letter shows that in India the company traded on the emperor's terms; the English text is a contemporary version whose translator is not named.

This Dutch account, published by Taiwan's last Dutch governor and his associates under the title Neglected Formosa, blames the company's leaders for losing the island and reports Koxinga's words second-hand. Koxinga's charge that the company's friendship lasted only while it brought advantage gives an Asian ruler's view of company behaviour, filtered through Dutch authors.

Davenant, an English writer on trade and public finance, wrote this essay on the East India trade for English readers, and here he states what England expected from its colonies. It is strong evidence of mercantilist thinking about colonies as buyers of English goods and suppliers of what England could not grow, but it gives no colonial view.

Montesquieu, a French philosopher writing in 1748, sums up the European rule that only the mother country may trade with its colonies and defends it as payment for protection. As a general summary from near the end of the period it shows how settled the system had become, though it gives no colonist's view.

Blande, a London merchant, petitions the king for the planters of Virginia and Maryland and wants the Navigation Act lifted for them, so he describes its effects in the darkest terms. His details on prices still show how the law let a few English traders fix what planters paid and received.

Berkeley was Virginia's royal governor answering official questions from the king's commissioners, so his attack on the Navigation Act carries weight: even a crown official thought it harmed the colony. His remark that New Englanders broke the law shows that mercantilist rules were not always obeyed.

thesis: Mercantilism shaped how European states ran their empires to a great extent because it guided their laws: England's Navigation Acts and Spain's limits on the Manila trade aimed to keep trade and bullion inside each empire, and writers from Mun to Montesquieu described colonies as markets and suppliers for the mother country.

Mercantilism shaped what joint-stock companies were allowed to do more than what they could do in Asia: states gave companies monopolies and the right to build forts, make alliances and appoint governors, yet in India and Taiwan the English and Dutch had to accept the terms of strong Asian rulers such as Jahangir and Koxinga.

Mercantilism's hold on colonies was real but limited, because the people it governed protested or evaded it: Virginia's own governor called the Navigation Act destructive and admitted that New Englanders broke it, and Spanish officials let the Manila trade exceed its legal limits.

contextualization.text: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly found lands between Spain and Portugal, but no other European power facing the Atlantic ever accepted it, so the Dutch, English and French built their empires by challenging the Iberian claims.

From the 1500s to the 1700s European governments treated wealth as limited and trade as a contest between rivals, and they regulated their economies to increase state power, which made mercantilism the economic partner of absolute monarchy.

outsideEvidence.text: Dutch East India Company (VOC), founded in 1602: the Dutch government gave it a trade monopoly from the Cape of Good Hope to the Strait of Magellan and the right to make treaties, build forts and keep armed forces, the clearest case of a company acting like a state.

Jean-Baptiste Colbert's policies in France: Louis XIV's finance minister raised protective tariffs and founded the French East India and West India companies in 1664, though they struggled to attract enough capital, which shows mercantilism as a French state project with mixed results.
Anglo-Dutch Wars: commercial rivalry caused the first three wars between 1652 and 1674, and the first grew out of the Navigation Act of 1651, which shows that mercantilist laws could lead to war.

Molasses Act of 1733: Parliament taxed foreign molasses to give British West Indian sugar growers a near monopoly of the American market, but New Englanders largely got around it by smuggling and bribing customs officials.

Casa de Contratación, set up in Seville in 1503: this royal agency oversaw trade with the Americas, scheduled ships and routes and collected duties, which shows that Spain ran colonial trade through the state itself.

complexity: Explain similarity and difference: the Dutch and English both chartered companies with the power to build forts and make war, but the Dutch lawyer Grotius argued in 1609 that the seas were free to all traders, a useful claim against Spanish and Portuguese monopolies, while England's Navigation Acts closed English trade to the Dutch.

Corroborate across groups: Mun's rule that a kingdom must sell more than it buys (state policy) and Montesquieu's 'fundamental law' that only the mother country may trade with its colonies state the same logic about a century apart (Mun wrote c. 1630), which shows how lasting mercantilist thinking was.
Connect to a later period: Adam Smith attacked mercantilism in The Wealth of Nations (1776), and British trade restrictions on the colonies became one of the causes of the American Revolution.

prompt: Evaluate how East Asian states responded to European traders and missionaries in the period 1550–1750.

groups.label: Interest in European knowledge and skills

pool.sourcing: Hideyoshi, who was unifying Japan, accuses the missionaries of preaching against Japanese law and destroying temples, yet lets Portuguese merchants stay, so the edict separates religion from trade. It is strong evidence of his stated reasons, but the English comes from Murdoch's 1903 translation of a European version and may differ from the Japanese original.

Hamel, a Dutch company bookkeeper shipwrecked on Korea in 1653 and held there until 1666, reports what a long-held Dutch sailor and the Korean king told the captives. His account is strong evidence that Korea kept foreigners from leaving, though it gives only a captive's view and no Korean explanation of the rule.

The shogun's councillors meant this sentence as a warning that would reach 'Macao and even the country of Europe', so its harshness was the point. It is strong evidence of how far Japan went to stop Portuguese contact, but it reaches us only through Murdoch's 1903 English version of European accounts by the Jesuit Cardim and others.

Kangxi wrote this comment in anger after reading the papal decree that forbade Chinese Christians to honour Confucius and their ancestors, so his contempt for 'Westerners' answers a specific challenge to Chinese custom. It shows that the ban on preaching followed a dispute over Chinese rites; the English is a modern translation (Dan J. Li, 1969).

Xavier writes to fellow Jesuits in Goa and wants to show the mission succeeding, so he stresses the lord's delight and goodwill. Read with care, it shows that preaching in Yamaguchi depended on a local lord's licence, which he gave after receiving the missionaries' letters and presents.

This ruling of the Board of Rites, approved by Kangxi, states official policy, and it allows Christian worship because the Europeans 'do not excite any disturbances'. That reasoning shows toleration depended on good behaviour in the state's eyes; the English version was quoted by Neill (1964) and its translator is not named.

Xu Guangqi, a Ming official who had become a Christian, proposes this test while defending the Jesuits against accusers in the Board of Rites, so he offers terms the court could accept. It shows how contact could be placed under the judgment of the emperor's ministers and the Confucian classics, though Xu clearly expected the Jesuits to pass.

Kaempfer, a German physician serving the Dutch company at Nagasaki, wrote this after returning to Europe, and his phrase 'almost perpetual imprisonment' shows a European's resentment. It is strong evidence of the terms the Dutch accepted to keep trading, from life on a guarded island to hiding every outward sign of Christianity.

Adams, an English pilot shipwrecked in Japan, writes to his countrymen and may stress his own favour at court. Still, his account of building Ieyasu a European-style ship and teaching him geometry is good evidence that Japan's ruler valued useful European skills, though the claim to have taught Ieyasu geometry rests on Adams's word alone.

Xu Guangqi was a Christian convert who had worked with the Jesuits, writing to the emperor to protect them, so his high praise is advocacy. It is still strong evidence that a respected Ming scholar-official valued European arts and sciences.

Kaempfer reports questions put to him in person at the Dutch audience in Edo, though he wrote them down years later in Europe. The shogun's questions about medicine and his order for a remedy from Batavia show interest in European knowledge inside a tightly controlled form of contact.

Du Halde was a Jesuit in Paris who compiled other missionaries' reports and never saw China, and he wanted to show the mission in a good light. His account is useful evidence of how the Jesuits used science to win Kangxi's protection but weaker evidence of Kangxi's own motives.

thesis: East Asian states responded mainly by controlling contact on their own terms: rulers kept the trade and knowledge they found useful and restricted missionaries when Christianity seemed to threaten order, as Hideyoshi's edict keeping Portuguese merchants and Kangxi's shift from toleration in 1692 to a preaching ban in 1721 show.

Responses moved from openness toward restriction, fastest in Japan: local lords licensed preachers in the 1550s, Hideyoshi ordered missionaries out in 1587, and after the shogunate banned Portuguese ships in 1639, the Dutch were the only Europeans left, confined from 1641 to the island of Dejima, while China kept Jesuits at court for their science and Korea simply kept foreigners from leaving.

Rulers' interest in European knowledge never became acceptance of European religion or power: Ieyasu used Adams's shipbuilding, the shogun questioned Kaempfer about medicine and Kangxi enjoyed the Jesuits' science, yet each limited where Europeans could go and what they could preach.

contextualization.text: Tokugawa Ieyasu founded a shogunate at Edo in 1603 that put political stability first, and its leaders came to see Catholic missionaries as a tool of Spanish and Portuguese colonial expansion in Asia and a threat to their rule.

In 1644 the Manchus took Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty, and under Kangxi (reigned 1661–1722) the empire grew and made a border treaty with Russia at Nerchinsk in 1689, so the Qing dealt with Europeans from a position of strength.

outsideEvidence.text: Matteo Ricci: this Italian Jesuit learned Chinese, adopted Chinese culture, made a world map for Chinese scholars and was allowed to live in Beijing from 1601, which shows that Ming China accepted missionaries who came as scholars.

Ferdinand Verbiest: this Jesuit astronomer directed the Qing Imperial Board of Astronomy and advised the emperor on making more than 300 cannon, which shows that the Qing put European expertise to the state's use.

Shimabara Rebellion (1637–38): a revolt of heavily taxed peasants, many of them Catholics, that the shogunate crushed with help from a Dutch ship and then answered by enforcing its ban on Christianity more strictly.

Sakoku edicts of the 1630s: from 1635 Japanese were forbidden to sail abroad or to return from overseas, which shows that the shogunate restricted its own people's contact with the outside world as well as Europeans'.
Twenty-six Martyrs of Japan (1597): on Hideyoshi's orders, 26 Catholics were arrested and then crucified at Nagasaki, which shows that his expulsion policy turned violent.

Rangaku ('Dutch learning'): after the shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune relaxed the ban on Western books in 1720, Japanese scholars translated Dutch works on medicine and science, which shows interest in European knowledge growing under seclusion.

complexity: Explain similarity and difference: Japan and China both welcomed European knowledge and limited missionaries, but Japan expelled the Portuguese and executed Christians, while the Qing kept some Jesuits at court as astronomers and artists even after the 1721 ban.

Qualify with a counter-argument: Europeans shaped these responses too, since the Protestant Dutch hid their Christianity to keep trading in Japan while the Pope's ruling against Chinese rites provoked Kangxi's ban, so restriction often answered European choices.

Connect to a later period: control on East Asian terms ended in the 1800s, when Britain defeated China in the Opium War (1839–42) and Commodore Matthew Perry's arrival in 1853 pressed Japan to open its ports.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which Indigenous peoples resisted European colonization in the Americas in the period 1492–1750.

pool.sourcing: These Nahua accounts were recorded in Nahuatl in the decades after 1521 from the Mexica side, and they present the attack on the Spaniards as a just answer to a treacherous massacre. They are strong evidence of how the Mexica remembered and justified their war, though the English comes from a 1962 translation made through Spanish.

A Kaqchikel Maya noble wrote these annals for his own people ('O my children'), so he explains the revolt as a response to Alvarado's demands for gold and threats to burn the chiefs. It is strong evidence of why and how the Kaqchikel fought, with trenches and pits against horses, though it was written decades later and Brinton credits this early part to the author's father.

Pedro Pizarro was one of the Spaniards inside Cuzco during the siege, writing 35 years later, so his picture of a huge army also makes the Spanish survival look heroic. Even so, an enemy's description of Manco Inca's army and its burning of the city is strong evidence of large-scale armed resistance.

Rowlandson, an English colonist taken captive, wrote to show God's hand in her ordeal, so she credits the Lord with keeping her captors fed. Her admission that they mocked the slow English army and survived every effort to starve them is strong evidence of Native military skill in King Philip's War, coming from an enemy.

Powhatan's speech was written down in English by colonists who served under John Smith and published in 1612, so its words are theirs and may be shaped to show Smith's dealings well. Its argument that the English would starve if his people hid their food and fled shows a leader using the colony's need for Powhatan food as bargaining power.

The Jesuit Vimont recorded this speech for French readers, who welcomed peace with the Mohawk, so it passes through a French observer's eyes and translation. The wampum collars and ritual gestures he describes show the Haudenosaunee negotiating by their own diplomatic customs.

Easton, Rhode Island's deputy governor, met Metacom's council days before the war while trying to settle the quarrel, and he records their grievances in detail. That makes the passage strong evidence that the Wampanoag stated their case before fighting, though their words reach us through an English writer.

These are official treaty minutes, interpreted by Conrad Weiser and printed by Benjamin Franklin, so Canassatego's words passed through an interpreter and a colonial printer. They are strong evidence that the Six Nations defended their land claims in colonial councils by citing their ancestry and their earlier agreements with the Dutch.

Molina, a Spanish priest in Cuzco who preached in Quechua, describes Taki Onqoy from the side of the church it attacked. Because he had no reason to invent a movement against his own faith, his account is strong evidence that Andean preachers urged people to reject baptism, Christian names and Spanish things.

Ávila was a parish priest campaigning against Andean religion, so he had every reason to report success. His admission that his parishioners still kept their traditions 'most inviolably' is therefore strong evidence that Andean beliefs survived more than seventy years after the conquest.

Garcilaso, son of a conquistador and an Inca noblewoman, recalls conversations he heard as a boy in Cuzco and wrote them down decades later in Spain to honour Inca history. The passage shows Inca families keeping the memory of their empire alive in private, a quiet form of cultural resistance.

Brébeuf wrote for the Jesuit Relations, which were printed in France for supporters of the mission, so he reports hopeful signs alongside Wendat refusals. His account of a man who blended Christian teaching with Wendat beliefs and chose to join his ancestors shows resistance through selective adoption.

thesis: Indigenous peoples resisted European colonization to a great extent and in many forms: the Mexica, Kaqchikel and Inca fought large wars, the Powhatan and Haudenosaunee bargained with food, land claims and diplomacy, and Andean communities kept their own religion alive under Spanish rule.

Armed resistance usually failed where disease and Indigenous allies helped the Spanish, so the most lasting resistance was cultural: Taki Onqoy preachers rejected baptism in the 1560s, and in 1608 the priest Ávila admitted that Andean traditions were still kept 'most inviolably'.

The form of resistance depended on how much power a people still held: nations that kept their land and could play rival Europeans against each other, such as the Six Nations at Lancaster in 1744, resisted through negotiation, while peoples already under colonial rule, like the Andeans, resisted through hidden religion and memory.

contextualization.text: Smallpox, measles, influenza and other diseases from Eurasia and Africa swept through Native American populations, which fell by an estimated 50 to 95 percent by 1650, depending on the region, weakening every kind of resistance.

Cortés overthrew the Aztec Empire between 1519 and 1521 with a small Spanish force and a large army of Indigenous allies such as the Tlaxcalans, so Indigenous peoples fought on both sides of the conquest.

ref.title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

contextualization.text: In northeastern North America the Iroquois Confederacy played a strategic role in the struggle between France and Britain, and it persuaded colonial governments to use Iroquois rituals in their joint negotiations.

outsideEvidence.text: Pueblo Revolt (1680): led by Popé, the Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for 12 years and destroyed churches, which shows armed and religious resistance working together.

Mapuche resistance in Chile: Mapuche villages formed military alliances and their warriors learned to fight with horses, and they resisted Spanish and later Chilean rule for about 350 years, which shows that armed resistance could last.
Neo-Inca State at Vilcabamba (1537–1572): after the siege of Cuzco, Manco Inca set up an independent Inca state that lasted until the Spanish captured and executed Túpac Amaru in 1572.

Powhatan War (1622–44): as settlers pressed onto Powhatan land to grow tobacco, Opechancanough led a surprise attack in 1622 that killed 347 of about 1,200 colonists, which shows bargaining giving way to war.

Mixtón War (1540–42): the Caxcan people rose to push the Spanish out of northwestern Mexico after years of killing and enslavement, which shows armed resistance in New Spain after the fall of the Aztecs.
Great Peace of Montreal (1701): New France and 39 Native nations signed a treaty that ended the Beaver Wars, which shows negotiation on a large scale.

complexity: Corroborate across groups: Powhatan's threat to hide food and flee to the woods (negotiation) and Rowlandson's admission that the English could not starve their enemies (war) both show that knowledge of the land gave Native peoples leverage in diplomacy and in fighting.

Qualify with a counter-argument: many Indigenous peoples allied with Europeans against their own rivals, as the Tlaxcalans did with Cortés, and most Indigenous words in these documents were recorded by Europeans, so the sources show resistance mainly as Europeans chose to record it.
Connect to a later period: resistance continued after 1750, in Pontiac's War (1763) against the British around the Great Lakes and in the rebellion led by Túpac Amaru II in Peru (1780–81).

prompt: Evaluate the causes of rebellions and other challenges to state power in the period c. 1450–1750.

pool.sourcing: The Twelve Articles were a printed manifesto meant to win support and show that the peasants' demands were Christian, so they put the Gospel first. The demand that each community choose its own pastor shows how Reformation ideas gave peasants a religious reason to challenge their lords.

Molina, a Spanish priest in Cuzco who preached in Quechua, describes Taki Onqoy from the side of the church it attacked. His account shows that Andean preachers promised the huacas would restore the time of the Incas, good evidence that religion could drive a challenge to Spanish rule.

The besieged rebels wrote this letter to the shogun's commanders to justify their rising, so they stress persecution and deny wanting land. It is strong evidence that the rebels themselves named religion as their cause, though they had every reason to present the revolt in the best light.

Guru Gobind Singh wrote this Persian letter to Aurangzeb after his sons were killed and he had withdrawn from Anandpur, so it is a defiant protest from a religious leader at war with the emperor. It shows Sikh resistance framed in religious terms, as an answer to oaths broken in God's name; the English is Macauliffe's 1909 translation.

Retz was a leader of the Fronde and an enemy of Cardinal Mazarin, writing his memoirs about thirty years later, so he blames the finance minister Emeri and mocks Mazarin. His account is good evidence that new taxes angered Parisians, but his personal hostility colours his judgments.

Parliament presented this petition to Charles I to defend its own right to approve taxes, so it presents forced loans as illegal and those jailed for refusing as victims. It shows that disputes over taxation without consent drove the conflict between king and Parliament.

Koeckebacker headed the Dutch trading post at Hirado and wrote to his superior, the governor-general, so he had no stake in defending the Catholic rebels. His focus on impossible rice taxes and the lords' cruelty offers an outsider's view that economic hardship caused the revolt.

This letter protests the jizya to Aurangzeb by arguing that his peasants and treasury were already ruined, so it mixes economic and religious complaints to persuade. Some historians attribute it to Rana Raj Singh of Mewar, so it is safest read as evidence of how Hindu rulers argued against the tax.

Busbecq was the ambassador of the Habsburgs, the Ottomans' great rivals, and he reports what he learned at Suleiman's court. His account shows that rivalry between Suleiman's sons and the sympathy of Janissaries could fuel a revolt, though he could not see the plotting directly.

Aguirre had already renounced his loyalty to the king, so he justifies his war by claiming that royal officials robbed the men who won the empire. The letter shows how some conquistadors resented crown officials taking power and rewards, though his own rebellion was small and short.

The States General issued this declaration to justify rejecting Philip II, so it argues in general terms that a prince who breaks 'ancient customs and privileges' becomes a tyrant. It is strong evidence of the provinces' stated legal case, though this passage leaves out the religious conflict between Protestant rebels and the Catholic king that also drove the revolt.

Easton recorded Wampanoag complaints while trying to prevent war, and he sets them out in detail. They show that colonists choosing their own 'kings' for the Wampanoag and getting land from them undermined the sachems' authority and pushed Metacom toward war.

thesis: Taxes and economic hardship were the most common cause of challenges to state power, because rulers paying for wars and courts demanded more than subjects could give: Shimabara farmers faced impossible rice taxes, Parisians rejected new tariffs, Parliament protested forced loans, and the letter attributed to Shivaji tied the jizya to ruined peasants.

Religion was the cause that turned grievances into lasting movements, because it gave rebels a higher law to appeal to: German peasants cited the Gospel, Shimabara's rebels died for the 'Lord of Heaven', Guru Gobind Singh defied Aurangzeb, and Andean preachers promised the return of the huacas.

Many of the most serious challenges began when rulers centralized power at the expense of local elites with their own rights: the Dutch provinces, conquistadors like Aguirre and Wampanoag sachems all resisted a distant authority, and an Ottoman succession struggle shows rivals for power gathering followers, and economic or religious complaints gave them followers.

contextualization.text: Historians who describe a 'military revolution' argue that gunpowder weapons and new tactics in the 1500s and 1600s made armies larger, permanent and much more expensive, which pushed rulers to find new money and build stronger governments.

The Reformation, traditionally dated from Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses in 1517, split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches and had far-reaching political effects, giving subjects religious reasons to resist rulers.

outsideEvidence.text: Li Zicheng's rebellion: who joined the rebels in 1630 as famine spread in northern China, Li took Beijing in 1644 and brought down the Ming dynasty, a case where economic disaster fed rebellion.

Stenka Razin's revolt (1670–71): Cossacks and peasants, the peasants driven by hatred of serfdom (made law in 1649), rose along the Volga against Russia's nobles and officials, though not against the tsar himself.

Pueblo Revolt (1680): after missionaries burned sacred objects and Spanish authorities punished medicine men, Popé led the Pueblos to drive the Spanish out of New Mexico for 12 years, a revolt with clear religious causes.

English Civil Wars (1642–51): Charles I's 'ship money' levy without Parliament's approval and his church reforms, including a new prayer book that set off riots in Scotland in 1637, led to war between king and Parliament.

Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba: from the 1620s she fought Portuguese expansion in Angola, allied with the Dutch West India Company in 1641 and fought on until a peace treaty in 1656, an outside challenge to Portuguese colonial power.

complexity: Explain similarity and difference: the Shimabara Rebellion and the German Peasants' War were both peasant risings that joined religion to complaints about taxes and rents, but Japan's rebels were persecuted Christians facing a non-Christian state, while Germany's peasants used Reformation ideas against Christian lords.

Corroborate within one event: the Shimabara rebels' letter names religion as their cause while Koeckebacker blames taxes, which suggests that causes overlapped and that each source stressed the cause that suited its purpose.

Connect to a later period: the Petition of Right's claim that taxes need Parliament's consent was repeated in the English Bill of Rights (1689) and echoed by American colonists who protested taxation without representation in the 1760s and 1770s.
